title: Helping helps the helper
hookLine: volunteering is linked to better wellbeing in many studies, though cause and effect are hard to prove

cards: A stroller carried up the subway stairs. A hard night sat through with a friend. A Saturday at a food bank.
And then the walk home afterward. Volunteers asked about that walk often reach for the same words: better, lighter, sometimes better off than the person they helped.
That can feel almost like cheating, as if service should cost something. Researchers have tried to measure it, and they keep finding a pattern, with a catch.

teach.b: In the late nineteen eighties, a writer named Allan Luks surveyed thousands of volunteers. Many described the same thing: a warm rush while helping, then a longer calm. He called it the helper's high, and the name stuck.
In a 2008 study, researchers handed people envelopes of cash, five or twenty dollars, and told some to spend it on themselves and others to spend it on someone else by evening.
The ones who spent it on others were happier at the end of the day, and the amount didn't seem to matter much. Then the long studies.
Across many countries, people who volunteer tend to report better wellbeing, and in some studies of older adults, volunteers even lived longer. Now the honest part, the one that's easy to skip.
Much of this research finds a link, not a proof. Healthier, happier people may simply be more likely to volunteer in the first place. Untangling cause and effect is hard, and good scientists say so.
So nobody can promise that helping will fix your mood. What the evidence allows is modest: for many helpers, helping and feeling better travel together.
A proverb in the Bible puts it in farm words: "he that watereth shall be watered also himself." And here's the catch. Help only to feel good, and you start watching yourself instead of the person.
The good feeling works best as a surprise, not a goal.
So notice it when it comes.

how: Many volunteers describe a warm lift after helping, and wellbeing researchers study it through surveys, experiments with small gifts, and long-term studies of people who volunteer.

o: the pride of being thanked in public for a gift
the burnout that hits people who help too much
the warm rush and calm many feel after helping

games.q: what goes with what — tap the pairs.
p: not the same as a proof

s: studies show for certain that volunteering makes people happier
many studies find a link; happier, healthier people may simply volunteer more.
in the envelope study, the amount of money didn't seem to matter much
five or twenty dollars: spending it on others lifted mood either way.
the good feeling works best as the goal of helping
help only to feel good and you start watching yourself; it works best as a surprise.

games.q: you're a researcher. volunteers in your survey are happier than non-volunteers. what can you honestly say?
o: there's a link; cause and effect are hard to prove.
games.why: there's a link, not a proof. happier, healthier people may be more likely to volunteer in the first place.

practice: Bring back a time you helped someone, recently or long ago, and replay the moment right after. Where did you feel it, the chest, the face, the shoulders, and was it warmth, relief, tiredness, or nothing much?
All of it is information, so just notice, without grading it.

wordCard.voice: Helper's high, the warm rush and longer calm that researcher Allan Luks found many volunteers feel. Today's word.

carryVoice: Your line: it comes back. The person first, the feeling after. That's day one hundred forty.
